readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 15:1-17:29. Absalom leads a rebellion, and David flees Jerusalem. Notice how David responds, and how God works behind the scenes through Hushai and Ahithophel.
settingTheScene: Absalom has spent years winning the hearts of the people at the city gate. At last he declares himself king at Hebron, and David, hearing that “the hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom,” flees Jerusalem on foot. This is the setting for Psalm 3. These chapters are a long account of betrayal, loyalty, and the hidden hand of God.
observation: “Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel” (15:6).
David leaves the city, weeping, barefoot, with his head covered, and says, “If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back” (15:25-30).
Ittai the Gittite swears loyalty: “As the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king shall be, whether for death or for life, there also will your servant be” (15:21).
David prays, “O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness” (15:31).
Hushai pretends loyalty to Absalom, to counter Ahithophel’s advice (15:32-37; 17:5-14).
Shimei curses David, and David says, “Let him alone, and let him curse, for the LORD has told him to” (16:5-14).
“For the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, so that the LORD might bring harm upon Absalom” (17:14).
Ahithophel sets his house in order and hangs himself (17:23).
interpretation:
Absalom’s rebellion is the working out of Nathan’s prophecy. His method is subtle. He wins people by flattery, by promising justice, and by acting like a friend of the common man. It is a pattern of political manipulation as old as humanity: a man who “steals hearts” by appearing to offer what the king does not. He is charming, handsome, and ruthless.

David’s response is remarkable for its humility. He could fight. But he leaves the city, weeping, barefoot. He does not cling to the throne. Even the ark, which Zadok brings out, he sends back: “If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, he will bring me back… But if he says, I have no pleasure in you, behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him.” David has learned that he cannot manipulate God. He accepts whatever God decides.

His humility is tested by Shimei, who throws stones and curses him. David’s men want to kill Shimei. David says to leave him. Perhaps God has told him to curse. This is not weakness but a grasp that God may be using even insult to discipline him.

The contest between Ahithophel and Hushai shows God’s hidden providence. Ahithophel’s counsel was said to be like the word of God. David prays that it will be turned into foolishness. Hushai gives Absalom worse advice, and Absalom accepts it. The narrator tells us plainly: “The LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel.” God was at work behind the scenes, though no miracle was seen. Ahithophel, seeing that his advice was rejected, hangs himself.

The lesson is that God’s purposes are not defeated by human betrayal. He works through ordinary decisions, conversations, and even through bad advice.
connection: Jesus, too, left the city, crossed the Kidron, and went up the Mount of Olives weeping, and he was betrayed by one of his own counselors (2 Samuel 15:23, 30; John 18:1; Luke 22:47-48; Luke 19:41). Judas, like Ahithophel, hanged himself (Matthew 27:5). Jesus declared that the Father’s will would be done. And Romans 8:28 says that God works all things together for good.
application:
Practice David’s humility: in a conflict, ask, “What if God is using this to teach me?”

Think about a time when God’s hidden hand turned something for good, and thank him.

Pray, as David did, for wisdom and for confusion of plans that oppose his purposes.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to give you David’s humility when you are wronged.
Thank Jesus for being betrayed by his own for you.
Trust him with what is happening behind the scenes.
